glossary.title: Glossary
glossary.subtitle: Every term in plain words
glossary.intro: What the words in IA mean, and why they matter for your field.

waterDemand.plain: How much water the weather pulls out of a healthy, well-watered crop each day — hot, dry, windy and sunny days pull more. Scientists call it reference evapotranspiration (ET₀).
waterDemand.why: It tells you how fast your soil dries out, so IA can say when to irrigate and how much.

soilWater.plain: The water held in the soil around the roots that the crop can still take up. IA tracks it every day like a bank account: rain and irrigation pay in, the crop's water use pays out.
soilWater.why: When the 'easily available' part is used up, the crop starts to suffer and yield is lost.

easyWater.plain: The part of the soil water a crop can take up without effort. Once it is used, the plant closes its pores to save water and grows less.
easyWater.why: The best moment to irrigate is just before this part is used up.

greenness.plain: A satellite measure of how green and dense the plants are, from 0 (bare soil) to about 0.9 (thick, healthy crop).
greenness.why: It shows growth, harvests and weak spots in your field, even before you see them.

rainVsNormal.plain: Compares the rain of the last weeks with the same weeks in the past 40 years. Below zero means drier than usual, below −1.5 means very dry.
rainVsNormal.why: It shows quickly whether you are heading into a drought.

drought.plain: How dry your area is compared with normal, combining rain, crop water demand, soil moisture and plant greenness. Levels follow the U.S. Drought Monitor: D0 (abnormally dry) to D4 (exceptional).
drought.why: It helps you plan water use and choose drought-tolerant crops early.

cropWaterFactor.plain: How much water your crop uses compared with the 'crop water demand' of the weather. Small young plants use less, a full green canopy uses more. Scientists call it Kc.
cropWaterFactor.why: IA multiplies it with the weather to know your crop's real water use — and corrects it with satellite images of your field.

zones.plain: Parts of your field that always grow better or worse than the rest, found by an AI model from many satellite images and the terrain.
zones.why: Treat each zone on its own: sample soil, adjust seed or fertiliser, check drainage.

erosion.plain: How much soil heavy rain could wash away each year, estimated from slope, rain, soil and crop cover (the RUSLE method).
erosion.why: Bare soil on slopes loses fertility fast; cover crops and contour farming protect it.

wetness.plain: Where water collects in your field because of its shape — low, flat spots that drain a big area.
wetness.why: These spots stay wet, can waterlog, and are worth checking for drainage.

frostHollow.plain: A low spot where cold air sinks and collects on clear, calm nights.
frostHollow.why: Late spring and early autumn frosts hit here first — avoid frost-sensitive crops there.

rotation.plain: Growing different crops on the same field from year to year instead of the same crop again.
rotation.why: It breaks pest and disease cycles, adds nitrogen (with legumes) and builds healthier soil — often with higher yields.

nitrogen.plain: Nitrogen the next crop gets from the previous one (legumes like peas, beans and alfalfa leave nitrogen) minus what it still needs.
nitrogen.why: A positive balance means you can use less fertiliser.

breakCrop.plain: A crop from a different plant family that pests and diseases of your main crop cannot live on.
breakCrop.why: One or two years of a break crop starve soil-borne diseases and pests.

returnInterval.plain: The minimum number of years before the same crop (or its family) should be grown again on a field.
returnInterval.why: Growing it again too soon lets soil-borne diseases and pests build up.

confidence.plain: How sure IA is about a piece of advice, from the quality and resolution of the data behind it.
confidence.why: Low confidence means: check the field yourself before you act.

satellite.plain: NASA and European satellites measure rain, temperature, soil moisture and plant greenness every few days for the whole world.
satellite.why: It gives every farmer — even without sensors — a view of their field's water and growth.

yieldBadYear.plain: IA simulates your crop on the real weather of the last 15+ years at your field. 'Typical' is the middle result, 'bad year' is what 1 year in 10 gave.
yieldBadYear.why: Plan for the typical year, but make sure you can live with the bad one.
